title: Evenings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Developer sues over Gibraltar ban while Coldwater and others draft limits on power, noise and water use.

lines.text: Good evening, and welcome to Evenings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
Tonight we're digging into a federal lawsuit filed yesterday against the city of Gibraltar over its year-long data center moratorium.
That sounds like it could set a precedent for all these other towns we've been hearing about.
Exactly. CAL Realty and Raeden Acquisitions say the ban is an unlawful blanket prohibition that ignores their compliance with existing zoning.
So what's the bigger picture here? Why are so many communities hitting pause right now?
Residents keep raising the same concerns: massive power draws that could drive up electric bills, heavy water use for cooling, noise from the facilities, and pressure on farmland and local roads.
How long has this tension been building? It feels like more than just this week.
It's been accelerating this year. Towns like Kalamazoo just enacted a full-year moratorium yesterday after similar pushback on noise, power and water.
And Genoa Township extended theirs another year, right?
Yes, they voted to keep the freeze in place while they study impacts on roads, power and wells.
What does a typical moratorium actually accomplish for a small city?
It buys time to write permanent zoning rules that set limits on size, sound, setbacks and where these projects can even go.
Coldwater is doing something similar today, drafting rules to steer growth.
Township officials heard from a consultant on limiting building size, noise and power use. The draft would give local boards more say over locations.
Bay City is also moving on an ordinance with strict limits on size, sound and setbacks.
Residents even 30 miles away could feel changes in power rates and water use if big projects move forward anyway.
So the lawsuit in Gibraltar is really testing whether these pauses can hold up in court.
The developers argue it blocks projects that would otherwise meet zoning standards. A win for them could open doors that residents have been fighting on power and noise grounds.
Who are the main players in these fights across the state?
On one side, developers and companies looking for tax incentives and available land. On the other, city councils, residents and sometimes neighboring towns worried about infrastructure strain.
What kind of power demand are we talking about that makes electric bills a real issue?
These facilities can consume enormous amounts of electricity. Even mid-sized ones scale up fast, and that demand can affect rates for everyone on the grid.
Water use is another big one for cooling systems.
Exactly. Some proposals would pull significant volumes, raising questions about local wells and overall supply in certain areas.
And farmland conversion is part of the sprawl concern too.
Yes, especially in rural townships where large sites are easier to find but residents worry about losing agricultural land and seeing industrial development creep in.
Coldwater residents got their first look at plans and risks yesterday in an informational session.
Officials laid out potential jobs versus infrastructure strain, with concrete numbers on power and water demand.
The mayor there has already said there's no interest because of water and power use.
An MSU expert told the joint council meeting that consumption and property-value effects scale directly with facility size.
So they're planning new ordinances to discourage developers.
That's the pattern we're seeing: more towns moving from moratoriums to permanent rules.
What happens next in the Gibraltar case specifically?
The federal lawsuit will play out in court. It puts local tax incentives and land-use rules under scrutiny.
Could a ruling affect the other moratoriums happening right now?
Potentially. If the developers win, it might encourage more challenges elsewhere or push towns to craft tighter but defensible ordinances.
Meanwhile Mason residents are pushing back on a plan near the city.
They voiced worries about noise, traffic and electricity costs at a packed council meeting yesterday.
The council approved a public communication plan instead of rushing approvals.
That shows even smaller towns are now facing this pressure and choosing to slow down.
Kalamazoo also blocked new data centers and battery plants for a full year yesterday.
After residents raised alarms over the same issues: noise, power strain and water use.
It feels like a statewide wave of communities trying to get ahead of the buildout.
The lawsuit is the first big legal test of whether those pauses can stick.
What should listeners watch for in the coming weeks?
Court filings in Gibraltar, more ordinance votes like the ones in Coldwater and Bay City, and whether other developers file similar suits.
And how residents 30 or 60 miles away might start feeling the ripple effects on their own utility bills.
Exactly. The outcomes here could shape what these facilities look like across Michigan.
Thanks for laying that out. Let's move to some quick hits on the other stories from today and yesterday.
Coldwater residents got their first look at data center plans and risks in an informational session yesterday.
Branch County folks now have concrete numbers on jobs versus infrastructure strain.
Bay City is drafting rules to curb sprawl and noise with strict limits on size, sound and setbacks.
Genoa Township voted to extend its data center freeze another year while studying impacts.
Kalamazoo enacted its own one-year moratorium yesterday after resident concerns.
Mason residents pushed back at a packed meeting and the council approved a communication plan instead of quick approvals.
And another update: Mason City Council also approved that communication plan to keep residents informed.
Now let's look at what's on deck for listeners who want to attend meetings.
Tonight the Morley Village Council is taking up a data center proposal for the Morley dam site.
Also tonight, Ypsilanti Township Board of Trustees will vote on a six-month moratorium on power transmission infrastructure for data centers.
The Village of Morley Board has the same proposal discussion and vote on its agenda.
Tomorrow the Ypsilanti Planning Commission holds a public hearing and recommendation on zoning ordinance text amendments for data centers.
That includes definitions, permissible uses, performance standards, noise, water, energy and decommissioning rules.
And the City of Ypsilanti Planning Commission has a similar public hearing on zoning text amendments for data centers.
Plenty of chances for residents to weigh in directly.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker.
We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Gibraltar Lawsuit Tests Data Center Moratoriums as Towns Tighten Rules
